summary: Adds a way to advertise, using OSPF and IS-IS, whether a Path Computation Element supports PCEP security mechanisms such as TLS. Without this, clients discovering PCEs through the IGP could not tell whether a secure session was possible.

plainLanguage.summary: A shop posts a sign saying whether it has a safe, locked entrance, so customers know before they walk over.

questions: how to advertise pcep tls support
pced extensions for ospf and is-is
how does a client know a pce supports tls
what is the tcp-ao capability flag
subtitle: Lets OSPF and IS-IS announce whether a path computation server supports TLS or TCP-AO for PCEP.

tldr.problem: A client finding a Path Computation Element through IGP flooding could not tell whether the PCE supports TLS or TCP-AO, which it needs to know before opening a PCEP session.
tldr.mechanism: Two new capability flag bits in the PCE-CAP-FLAGS sub-TLV announce TCP-AO and PCEP over TLS support, and two new sub-TLVs, KEY-ID and KEY-CHAIN-NAME, carry TCP-AO key information.
tldr.outcome: Clients can check the advertised flags before connecting, and the RFC recommends securing PCEP with TLS and protecting the advertisement with IGP authentication.

today: RFC 9353 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2023. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It updates RFC 5088, RFC 5089, RFC 8231 and RFC 8306.

sections.title: The Problem: Securing PCEP Before It Starts
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes paths, and clients talk to it using PCEP. An attacker who intercepts PCEP messages could obtain sensitive information about computed paths and resources. RFC 5440 mentions protections, and TLS and the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO) are two of them.

A client (PCC) needs to know whether a PCE server supports TLS or TCP-AO before it connects, as Section 4 of RFC 8253 requires. RFC 5088 (OSPF) and RFC 5089 (IS-IS) let a PCE advertise its capabilities by IGP flooding but had no way to advertise security support.

The PCEP Open message is another way to discover capabilities, but the TCP security key parameters must be known before the session exists and Open messages are exchanged. That is why the IGP is used.
sections.plainLanguage: You need to know whether a door is locked the safe way before you walk up to it, so the sign has to be posted where you can read it from afar.

sections.title: Two New Capability Flags
sections.content:
The RFC defines two capability flag bits in the PCE-CAP-FLAGS sub-TLV: one for TCP-AO support and one for PCEP over TLS support. IS-IS reuses the same flags as OSPF.

A PCE that supports TCP-AO SHOULD set the TCP-AO bit, and one that supports TLS SHOULD set the TLS bit. If it supports several mechanisms, it SHOULD set all corresponding bits.

A client may be configured to require a given security capability. If so, it MUST verify that the matching flag bit is set for that server before it opens a connection to it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each lock type gets its own checkbox on the sign. A shop with two kinds of locks ticks both boxes, and a picky customer checks the box before walking in.

sections.title: KEY-ID and KEY-CHAIN-NAME Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The KEY-ID sub-TLV (type 6) carries the one-octet KeyID from RFC 5925 that identifies the TCP-AO Master Key Tuple. In IS-IS its length is 1. In OSPF its length is 4 because of three reserved octets, which MUST be set to zero on sending and ignored on receipt.

The KEY-CHAIN-NAME sub-TLV (type 7) carries a key chain name of 1 to 255 octets. It MUST be encoded in UTF-8, is not NULL terminated, and requires UTF-8 shortest-form encoding. The name could be configured by command-line interface or installed in the YANG datastore. In OSPF the sub-TLV MUST be zero-padded to 4-octet alignment, and the padding is not counted in the Length field.

Either sub-TLV MAY be present in the PCED sub-TLV (IS-IS) or PCED TLV (OSPF) when the TCP-AO flag is set.
sections.plainLanguage: If the shop uses a key lock, it can also write on the sign which key number or which key ring to use.

sections.title: Updates to Earlier RFCs and Compatibility
sections.content:
RFC 5088 and RFC 5089 both said that no new sub-TLVs would be added to the PCED TLV. This RFC updates both to allow the two new sub-TLVs, calling it an exception justified by the need to discover PCEP security support before a session is set up. The old restrictions are otherwise still in place, and later needs should consider RFC 6823 or another mechanism.

The PCE Capability Flags registry moves to the Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) Parameters grouping. RFC 9353 therefore also updates RFC 8231 and RFC 8306 to point at it.

A router that does not understand the new bits or sub-TLVs silently ignores them, so no new interoperability issues arise.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rules said no new boxes on the sign. This makes one careful exception, and shops that cannot read the new boxes just skip them.

sections.title: Management Considerations
sections.content:
A PCE implementation SHOULD allow these parameters to be configured: support for TCP-AO, the KeyID used by TCP-AO, the key chain name, and support for TLS. Normal IGP operation meets the liveness detection and monitoring needs, and the advertised information can be checked against what the PCE stores using the PCEP YANG module.

Frequent changes in the advertised security information may significantly affect the IGP and could destabilize the network by making PCCs reconnect their sessions to PCEs.
sections.plainLanguage: If the shop keeps changing its sign all day, customers keep running back and forth. So change it rarely.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A PCEP speaker MUST support TCP MD5 per RFC 5440, so no capability bit is needed for it. TCP MD5 has since been obsoleted by TCP-AO, but TCP-AO is not widely implemented, so the RFC RECOMMENDS securing PCEP with TLS per RFC 8253. An implementation SHOULD offer at least one of the two capabilities defined here.

The new bits are open to a downgrade attack by setting them to zero, and the Key-ID or KEY-CHAIN-NAME contents could be altered to enable an on-path attack. So the IGP MUST be known to provide authentication and integrity for the PCED TLV, using RFC 5304, RFC 5310 or RFC 5709, before these parameters are advertised.

OSPF and IS-IS cannot protect the confidentiality of the PCED TLV, so operators must make sure KeyIDs and key chain names do not reveal sensitive network information.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could rub out the ticks on the sign or swap the key number, so the sign itself must be tamper-proof, and it must not give away secrets.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
IANA moved the Path Computation Element (PCE) Capability Flags registry into the Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) Parameters grouping and assigned bit 17 to TCP-AO Support and bit 18 to PCEP over TLS support.

IANA also created the PCE Discovery (PCED) Sub-TLV Type Indicators registry with the registration policy Standards Action, covering values 0 to 65535. It is filled with values 0 to 5 from RFC 5088 plus the new 6 (KEY-ID) and 7 (KEY-CHAIN-NAME).
sections.plainLanguage: The official list got two new tick boxes and a new numbered list of the kinds of notes the sign can hold.

fields.desc: Zero on sending, ignored on receipt.
